newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria plans to end fuel shortage with imports.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria plans to end fuel shortage with imports.

text.p: Nigeria said on Tuesday that 33 cargoes of oil products would arrive in the country between now and Sunday to end an acute fuel scarcity that has plagued Africa's leading oil-producing nation for the past five weeks.

"The cargoes will come from Europe, especially Spain as well as other African countries," Ibrahim Abubakar, the managing director of the Pipelines and Products Marketing Company (PPMC), a unit of the Nigerian National Petroleum Corp (NNPC), told reporters in Lagos.
Nigeria's military rulers ended an emergency meeting in the capital Abuja on Monday night pledging to end the crisis within 48 hours.
Although Nigeria frequently experiences fuel shortage the current crunch has been the most serious since a 1994 strike by oil workers.
It has caused serious hardship for thousands of commuters, many of whom had to trek to work. Many businesses have closed temporarily.
Abubakar said of the imports 24 cargoes would be petrol, five would be kerosene including aviation fuel, and four would be diesel.
"Starting from today, 24th June, 1997, we shall have in our system for distribution in Lagos, Ore, Ilorin and Ibadan depots over 120,000,000 litres of (petrol)," Abubakar said.
He said the first consignment of 30,000 tonnes of fuel would arrive in Nigeria at 10 p.m. (2100 GMT) on Tuesday and others would arrive on Friday and Sunday this week.
Motorists in Lagos have welcomed the government's promise of early action and said more filling stations appeared to have fuel on Tuesday.
"There are a few more stations with fuel today but the queues are still long," said bus driver Okechukwu Okeke, adding "We hope the government will keep to its word because we have suffered enough."

Allowing imports is a major climbdown by military ruler General Sani Abacha, who stopped fuel imports in September last year and ordered state-run Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation to get local refineries to work.
Nigeria produces about two million barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil and exports all of its production, except for 250,000 bpd allocated to its four refineries for processing into fuel products.

No exact reason has been given for the current shortage but it is no secret that the refineries have long been operating at a fraction of their 445,000 bpd installed capacity because of lack of maintenance and mismanagement.
The head of the manufacturing association warned of an imminent collapse of industries if the situation was not checked, labelling it "a national shame".
The black market cashed in on the shortage with touts charging several times the official pump price.

In Abacha's home state Kano, youths staged a peaceful protest on Monday to demand an immediate normalisation of the situation. University students warned of public protests if the situation was not redressed.
